Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't trust that I will do the right thing
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, funerals/cemeteries are not impossible triggers, but they are weakly anchored unless there was a death in the accident or major bereavement content. Nothing else in the profile suggests grief- or death-related cueing, so this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for a life-threatening accident. The other items center on fear, disorganization of memory, hypervigilance, and damaged self-view, but do not indicate betrayal by authorities, emergency response, or organizational negligence. This appraisal therefore appears insufficiently supported by the trauma context and accompanying items.

vignette: Leila is a 58‑year‑old psychiatrist of Māori descent who, after a divorce, lives alone in a quiet suburban house. On a rainy Tuesday in late spring, she was driving home from a conference when a semi‑truck swerved into her lane, sending her car into a ditch. The impact was severe enough that the airbags deployed, her ears rang, and she felt her body flip once before the truck slammed into a guardrail. The car burned for a moment, then extinguished, and Leila was left with bruises, a broken rib, and a hollowing sense of life abruptly curtailed. In the months that followed she began to notice that any sound or sight associated with traffic—an honking horn, a passing bus, even a reflection of a windshield—could trigger a rush of intrusive thoughts that painted the crash in brutal detail. Those moments would flash up with no warning, plunging her into a scene she could no longer piece together; the memory was a jumbled mosaic of sounds, smells, and a vague sense of falling. The fragmented recollection made it impossible to narrate a clear story of the day, and the chaos of the events fed Leila’s belief that she had been permanently altered, that she could no longer trust her own judgment. Each sudden car-related trigger thus reinforced her perception of a world that was dangerous, and the idea that she had become a fragile vessel who might fail at any moment. The sense that the world was hostile spurred Leila to a rigid set of coping strategies. She insisted on controlling her emotions, watching her face for any hint of fear or sadness, and she began to avoid situations that might arouse them, including sex and nights in bed where darkness might let her sense her body being vulnerable. Her conviction that she had been irrevocably harmed made her doubt her ability to act rightly, so she started to limit her exposure to anything that could remind her of the crash. Every time she heard the clatter of tires or saw a flashing light, her body’s startle response flared, and she would immediately turn her back toward a wall, positioning herself where she could see the whole room and feel physically safe. In the quiet of night she would wake abruptly, eyes wide, checking every door, every window, until she could confirm that nothing was amiss. Each of these threats amplified her urge to control, and her controlling, in turn, made her more alert and more susceptible to startle. The memory of the crash, fragmented as it was, would surface in moments of high anxiety, reinforcing her belief that she could not trust her own perception. The lack of a coherent story left her convinced that the event had forever damaged her, and that damage fed the very triggers that now haunted her. Leila’s avoidance of sleep has left her chronically exhausted, and her avoidance of intimacy has strained the brief, fragile relationships she keeps with friends. At work, where she often hears patients describing their own trauma, she now feels hyper‑vigilant: a patient’s mention of a car accident can send her heart racing, and she will instinctively pull a chair away from a window, sit with her back against the wall, and try to focus on clinical notes while her mind races to re‑experience the crash in the most jarring detail it can muster. Each of these moments, triggered by a seemingly innocuous comment, is a reminder of the traumatic image and a reinforcement of the belief that she is unsafe. Her compulsive need to check every exit in the office, her deliberate avoidance of dimly lit rooms, and her relentless monitoring of her own emotional state are all born from the conviction that she is permanently damaged and that the world is dangerous. These behaviors, in turn, keep her memory fragmented, her threats heightened, and her triggers ever present, creating a self‑reinforcing cycle that has made her life feel trapped in a perpetual state of wariness. Today, after another night of waking to the sound of a neighbor’s car reversing on the street, Leila finally decided to seek help. She tells her therapist that she has lost sleep for six months, that she cannot enjoy a conversation with her friend without feeling a surge of terror, and that her once‑vibrant professional confidence has eroded to a quiet fear of doing anything that might remind her of the crash. Her greatest fear now is that she will not be able to regain the sense of safety she once felt and that her career—and her sense of self—will continue to unravel. She hopes that by confronting the triggers and the memories that keep her locked in this state, she can break the loop and reclaim a life that feels possible.
